decisions.quote: This experiment has replicated the findings of Sonbul and Schmitt’s (2013) second experiment for the development of declarative knowledge of technical collocations. Both Sonbul and Schmitt’s experiment and my experiment found, firstly, that participants gained substantial declarative knowledge (as measured in the cued-recall and form-recognition tests) through repeated exposure to the collocations in supportive contexts in incidental learning conditions—both typographically enhanced and unenhanced—when compared with the control group’s results. The second replicated finding is that the presence of typographic enhancement of collocations led to greater retention than the absence of typographic enhancement.
decisions.location: Section 3.10.1.1, pp. 89-90 (see also Section 3.10.1.2, p. 90, and Sections 5.3.2-5.3.5, pp. 157-161)
decisions.reason: Across Chapter 3 (pp. 49, 52, 89-95) and Chapter 5 (pp. 148, 157-161), the thesis explicitly separates Experiment 1 into its conceptual replication component (declarative knowledge of technical collocations, Section 3.10.1.1) and its extension component (procedural knowledge under an increased repetition schedule, Section 3.10.1.2), while Experiment 2 is a further extension to non-technical collocations. In Section 3.10.1.1, the author states an explicit verdict that Experiment 1 replicated all four of Sonbul and Schmitt's (2013) declarative-knowledge findings (substantial gains from repeated exposure, superiority of typographic enhancement over unenhanced reading, retention over two weeks, and recognition exceeding recall). In Section 3.10.1.2 (p. 90), the author explicitly frames the procedural priming effect in the reading-only condition as an extension attributable to the new treatment dose (nine exposures across three sessions over two days versus Sonbul and Schmitt's three exposures in one session) that 'partly fulfils' Sonbul and Schmitt's (2013, p. 153) own prediction for the unenhanced condition, and concludes in Sections 3.10.2 and 5.3.2-5.3.5 that the declarative and procedural results corroborate Sonbul and Schmitt's claim of dissociation between declarative and procedural collocational knowledge.

decisions.quote: The results of the immediate cued-recall and form-recognition post-tests corroborate Sonbul and Schmitt’s findings: multiple encounters with the collocations produced substantial declarative collocational knowledge, and more declarative knowledge was produced through exposure to typographically-enhanced collocations (with and without glosses) than to typographically-unenhanced collocations.
decisions.location: Abstract, p. i (see also Section 3.10.1.1, p. 89)
decisions.reason: Experiment 1 is explicitly identified as the conceptual replication (and extension) of Sonbul and Schmitt (2013), and the author states an explicit overall verdict that it replicated and corroborated Sonbul and Schmitt's findings on declarative collocational knowledge, whereas Experiment 2 is an extension building on Experiment 1 with non-technical collocations.
